questions.prompt: A symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite when \(z^T M z\ge 0\) for every \(z\). For the 2 by 2 matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}\), that property holds exactly when
options: \(a\ge 0\), \(c\ge 0\), and \(ac\ge b^2\)
\(a\ge 0\) and \(c\ge 0\), with no condition on \(b\)
\(ac\ge b^2\), even if \(a\) is negative
\(b\ge 0\), with no condition on the diagonal
questions.explanation: Both diagonal entries must be nonnegative, and the determinant test \(ac-b^2\ge 0\) must hold as well. Nonnegative diagonal entries alone miss a large off-diagonal entry. The product test alone misses a negative diagonal. The sign of the off-diagonal entry is not the test: \(b\) is squared in \(ac\ge b^2\).

Here \(a=4\), \(b=1\), and \(c=4\), so \(ac-b^2=16-1=15\). Both diagonal entries are positive and the gap is positive, so \(M\) is positive definite. The product \(ac=16\) forgets to subtract \(b^2\). The trace \(a+c=8\) is a different symmetric function. The off-diagonal entry 1 is not the gap.

questions.prompt: The matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) has determinant \(1-4=-3\). It is
options: positive semidefinite, because both diagonal entries are positive
not positive semidefinite, because the determinant is negative
positive semidefinite, because the off-diagonal entries are positive
undefined as a semidefinite constraint, because the matrix is symmetric
questions.explanation: Positive diagonal entries are necessary and not sufficient. Here \(ac-b^2=-3<0\), so one eigenvalue is negative and the matrix is not positive semidefinite. The sign of the off-diagonal entries does not replace the determinant test. Symmetry is required for this constraint, and this matrix has it. The failure is the determinant, not the symmetry.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that turns \(t\ge x^2\) into a 2 by 2 semidefinite constraint by a block complement. Each step uses the matrix or the complement the previous step built.
questions.explanation: The matrix has to be filled before the complement of its leading entry is \(t-x^2\). That complement has to be formed before it can be required to be nonnegative. The conclusion \(t\ge x^2\) is what that requirement says, because the bottom-right entry is the positive number 1. Swapping an adjacent pair uses a complement or a conclusion that has not been formed.
steps: Place t, x, and the number 1 into the symmetric matrix with t and 1 on the diagonal and x off the diagonal.
Using the bottom-right entry 1, form the complement t-x^2.
Require that complement to be nonnegative, and keep the bottom-right entry positive.
Conclude that the matrix constraint holds exactly when t >= x^2.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest \(t\) such that \(\begin{bmatrix} t & 3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) is positive semidefinite?
questions.explanation: The bottom-right entry 4 is positive. The diagonal test also needs \(t\ge 0\), and the determinant test needs \(4t\ge 9\), so \(t\ge 9/4=2.25\). That lower bound is already positive, so it is the smallest feasible \(t\). The number 3 is the off-diagonal entry. The number 4 is the fixed diagonal entry. The product \(3\cdot 4=12\) is not the bound on \(t\).

questions.prompt: What is the smaller eigenvalue of \(\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)?
questions.explanation: The trace is 9 and the determinant is \(18-4=14\). The eigenvalues are the roots of \(\lambda^2-9\lambda+14=0\), which factors as \((\lambda-7)(\lambda-2)=0\). The roots are 7 and 2, so the smaller one is 2. Both are positive, and the matrix is positive definite. The trace 9 is the sum of the eigenvalues, not the smaller one. The off-diagonal entry 2 happens to equal the smaller eigenvalue in this matrix; the factorization is what identifies it.

questions.prompt: Let \(p>0\). What is the smallest \(t\) such that \(\begin{bmatrix} t & s \\ s & p \end{bmatrix}\) is positive semidefinite? Write it in \(s\) and \(p\).
questions.explanation:
The entry \(p\) is already positive. The determinant test says \(tp\ge s^2\), so \(t\ge s^2/p\). That quotient is nonnegative, so it also meets \(t\ge 0\). It is the smallest feasible \(t\).
• \(s^2\) forgets to divide by \(p\).
• \(p/s^2\) inverts the ratio.
• \(s/p\) drops a factor of \(s\).

questions.prompt: A semidefinite constraint asks an affine matrix to be positive semidefinite. The matrix in that constraint must be
options: symmetric, because the quadratic form does not see the skew part
triangular, with zeros below the diagonal
a permutation matrix
nonsymmetric, so that the off-diagonal entries can differ
questions.explanation: The quadratic form \(z^T M z\) depends only on the symmetric part of \(M\). The semidefinite constraint is stated for a symmetric matrix, and each coefficient matrix in the affine expression is symmetric. A triangular pattern, a permutation, or a nonsymmetric pair of off-diagonal entries is a different requirement.

questions.prompt: Which of these symmetric matrices are positive semidefinite?
options: \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\)
questions.explanation: The first matrix is diagonal with positive entries, so both eigenvalues are positive. The zero matrix gives \(z^T 0 z=0\), which meets \(\ge 0\), so it is positive semidefinite. The second has determinant \(4-9<0\), so one eigenvalue is negative. The fourth has a negative diagonal entry, so the corresponding standard-basis vector produces a negative square.

questions.prompt: One step below is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails. The matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} t & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
questions.explanation: Symmetry holds, the pivot 1 is positive, and the complement is \(t-2^2/1=t-4\). Nonnegativity of that complement is \(t\ge 4\), which is stronger than \(t\ge 0\). At \(t=0\) the determinant gap is \(-4\), so the matrix is not positive semidefinite. The false step drops the complement.
steps: The bottom-right entry equals 1, which is positive.
The complement relative to that entry is \(t-4\), so \(t\ge 4\) is required.
The matrix is positive semidefinite as soon as \(t\ge 0\), because the top-left entry is the only one that can fail.
reasons: The complement t-4 must be nonnegative, so t>=0 is not enough.
The bottom-right entry is negative, so the complement is undefined.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest \(t\) such that \(\begin{bmatrix} t & 6 \\ 6 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) is positive semidefinite?
questions.explanation: The bottom-right entry 2 is positive. The determinant test requires \(2t\ge 36\), so \(t\ge 18\). That bound is positive, so the diagonal test \(t\ge 0\) does not raise it. The off-diagonal entry 6 is not the bound. The product \(6\cdot 2=12\) forgets that the complement divides \(6^2\) by 2.

questions.prompt: A later problem chooses a positive definite shape matrix for the largest ellipsoid that fits inside a list of half-spaces. That problem is not itself the general spectrahedron. The shared piece is
options: a free nonsymmetric matrix with no definiteness requirement
a positive definite matrix used as a decision, which this skill tests with a semidefinite constraint
an absolute penalty on the center of the ellipsoid
a fixed-step gradient iteration
questions.explanation: The shape matrix has to be positive definite for the ellipsoid to have positive volume in every direction. Positive-definiteness is the strict form of the semidefinite constraint this skill studies. The ellipsoid problem adds a volume objective and half-space inequalities. It does not use an absolute penalty or a gradient iteration as the definition of the shape.
